subject: chemistry-1
question: A student tries to "balance" H2 + O2 -> H2O by rewriting the product formula as H2O2. What is wrong with this approach?

options.text: The mass on each side changes, but the identity of the product stays the same
The equation stays chemically valid because a subscript was changed, not a coefficient
The equation is acceptable because subscripts and coefficients both scale the product amount
The equation no longer describes water; it describes hydrogen peroxide, a different compound

explanation:
Subscripts specify the fixed composition of a compound, so changing one produces a different substance rather than a different quantity of the same substance. H2O and H2O2 differ by one oxygen atom per molecule and have entirely different chemical properties: water is stable and drinkable, hydrogen peroxide is a reactive oxidizer that decomposes readily. Balancing is legitimate only when correct formulas are held fixed and coefficients in front of them are adjusted.

ELI-10: A formula is the substance's identity; a coefficient is how many units of it are present. If a reaction needs more water, you write a larger number in front of H2O. Editing the subscript instead changes what the substance is, the way changing letters inside a word changes the word rather than giving you two copies of it.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)
